nameStory: The Green Serpent Star gets its name from its five long, snake-like arms that writhe and twist as it moves across the ocean floor. The 'green' refers to its distinctive olive-green to dark green coloration, while 'serpent star' describes how its flexible arms undulate like serpents when it crawls.
description: The Green Serpent Star is a type of brittle star, related to sea stars but with much thinner, more flexible arms. This marine creature has a small, disc-shaped central body (about 1 inch across) with five long, slender arms that can stretch 4-6 times the body width. Unlike chunky sea stars, serpent stars move by rapidly coiling and uncoiling their arms in a swimming motion. The entire animal typically spans 6-8 inches from arm tip to arm tip.

idTips.label: Arm Movement
idTips.description: Arms move in rapid, snake-like undulations rather than the slow hydraulic movement of sea stars - watch for quick, whip-like coiling motions

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Olive-green to dark green body and arms with lighter banding or mottled patterns - feels smooth and slightly slimy to touch

idTips.label: Central Disc
idTips.description: Small, round central body about the size of a quarter with distinct arm joints where the five arms attach - feels firm like cartilage

idTips.label: Arm Flexibility
idTips.description: Arms are incredibly flexible and can bend in complete loops - they'll often curl tightly around your finger if handled gently

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, non-spiny surface unlike many other brittle stars - arms feel like flexible rubber tubing covered in wet skin

idTips.label: Size Proportion
idTips.description: Arms are dramatically longer and thinner than the central disc, typically 4-6 times the disc diameter in length

habitat: Found in rocky subtidal zones and tide pools along New England's coast, typically hiding under rocks, in crevices, or among seaweed holdfasts. Prefers areas with good water circulation at depths from low tide line down to about 150 feet. Often discovered when turning over rocks in deeper tide pools or while snorkeling in rocky areas with kelp.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, often found in shallower areas during spring tides. Good time to spot them moving between hiding spots during mating season.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation season when warm waters bring them into shallower tide pools and they're most active during daylight hours.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper, more protected areas. Often found clustered under the same rocks.
seasonality.winter: Retreat to deeper waters or well-protected crevices. Rarely seen in accessible tide pools, become sluggish in cold water.

funFact: When a Green Serpent Star loses an arm to a predator, it can completely regrow the entire limb in just a few months - and if the detached arm contains enough of the central disc, it can grow an entirely new serpent star, essentially cloning itself!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other brittle stars, but Green Serpent Stars are distinguished by their smooth arms (no spines), green coloration, and particularly fluid movement. Memory trick: 'Green and smooth like a garden snake, spiny brittle stars are rough like a rake.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'serpent star,' these animals are echinoderms closely related to sea stars and sea urchins, not reptiles. The term 'brittle star' comes from their ability to easily break off arms when threatened - it's a defense mechanism, not a sign of fragility.
compareHints: **Note: Limited reference data available** - Green Serpent Stars appear to be the only Ophioderma species commonly found in New England waters. They differ from other regional brittle stars by having completely smooth arms without spines or scales, distinctive green coloration, and particularly graceful, fluid arm movements compared to the more jerky motions of spiny brittle stars.
